name: Turkesterone
lead: Turkesterone is a naturally occurring phytoecdysteroid, a plant steroid related to the molting hormones of insects, found in Ajuga turkestanica and several other plants, including Vitex species, Cyanotis arachnoidea, wheat and Rhaponticum acaule [1][2]. It is sold as a dietary supplement and promoted to bodybuilders as a natural anabolic, often described by sellers as an alternative to anabolic steroids [2][12].

Most of the supporting claims come from animal and cell research and from work on the related compound ecdysterone [2][3]. Wikipedia states that turkesterone is under laboratory research for anabolic effects through PI3K and AKT signalling and that its pharmacokinetics, bioavailability and effects in humans remain to be determined [1].

Human data specific to turkesterone are limited to small short-term studies. A 2024 preliminary study of acute doses in 11 men found no significant effects on IGF-1, resting metabolic rate or lipid and carbohydrate metabolism [4]. The compound is not an androgen in the usual sense; proponents describe an estrogen receptor beta-linked or non-androgenic route, a view that appears in forum discussion [12].
infobox: Ajuga turkestanica, Vitex spp., Cyanotis arachnoidea, Rhaponticum acaule [1]
Sold as a dietary supplement; not an approved drug

paras: Turkesterone is used by lifters in the hope of increased muscle growth, strength and recovery, and is sometimes added to cutting or 'natural' stacks and to TRT regimens. T Nation members describe trying it for experimentation, adding it to pre-workouts alongside laxogenin and ecdysterone, using it during a cut and taking it for its supposed effect on SHBG [13][14][15][16][17]. One forum poster says turkesterone has 'even more fakes' than a related supplement [18].

A 2024 review of ecdysterone and turkesterone describes their potential in sport and nutrition and in conditions such as chronic fatigue, cardiovascular and neurodegenerative disorders, largely on preclinical evidence [3].

A preliminary study of multiple acute turkesterone doses in 11 healthy men reported no significant main effects on serum IGF-1, resting metabolic rate or lipid and carbohydrate metabolism, although IGF-1 was numerically higher with turkesterone; the authors said the data do not fully support turkesterone as a potent anabolic supplement but are foundational for further work [4]. A review titled 'Phytoecdysteroids do not have anabolic effects in skeletal muscle' has also been published [5], and a trial of an ecdysteroid supplement examined physical and mental performance indices [6]. Grokipedia reports additional 2024 and 2025 randomised trials with no improvement in muscle growth or performance, a claim from an AI-generated source that was not independently verified [2].

Grokipedia says animal studies indicate low toxicity [2]. One T Nation poster reports that taking turkesterone at night raised blood pressure and heart rate somewhat and worsened sleep scores for them, so they moved to mornings [19]. Long-term human safety has not been established in the sources cited. Another forum poster describes concern about teenagers in a gym discussing SARMs, turkesterone, testosterone and trenbolone [20].

Turkesterone has a polyhydroxylated structure on a cyclopentanoperhydrophenanthrene skeleton similar to cholesterol-derived steroids [1]. Proposed anabolic action runs through PI3K and AKT signalling [1]; forum posts describe a pathway different from conventional steroids and claim it increases SHBG [12][16]. Pharmacokinetics, bioavailability and human effects are listed as undetermined by Wikipedia [1]. Related lab work includes studies of minor ecdysteroids from Ajuga turkestanica and 1970s Soviet experiments comparing turkesterone with the anabolic steroid nerobol in rat liver [7][8].

Ecdysone was found in silkworm pupae in 1954 by Adolf Butenandt and Peter Karlson, and turkesterone was first reported in 1973 from Ajuga turkestanica by a team in Tashkent, with its structure elucidated in 1975, according to Grokipedia [2]. A 1978 Soviet paper studied turkesterone and nerobol effects on mouse liver protein synthesis [8]. In forum culture, a 2021 thread notes that turkesterone was 'becoming very popular (again)', citing old mouse studies that reported it was more effective than Dianabol in mice [21].

Human studies of turkesterone itself are few: a 2024 preliminary investigation of multiple acute doses on IGF-1 and metabolic rate in 11 men [4], a trial of an ecdysteroid supplement on performance indices [6], and, according to Grokipedia, further 2024 to 2025 randomised trials [2]. Reviews of ecdysteroids in sport are available [3][5]. Animal work includes rodent studies of phytoecdysteroids as erythropoiesis stimulators and of Rhaponticum extracts on adipogenesis [9][10].

timeline.event: Ecdysone is isolated from silkworm pupae by Butenandt and Karlson (per Grokipedia) [2].
Turkesterone is first reported from Ajuga turkestanica in Tashkent (per Grokipedia) [2].
Soviet study compares turkesterone with nerobol on mouse liver protein synthesis [8].
Review of ecdysterone and turkesterone in sport and nutrition [3]; preliminary acute-dose study in 11 men [4].

lore.intro: On T Nation turkesterone is discussed as a hyped 'natural anabolic', with members split between experimenting with it and describing it as ineffective [15][22][21].

claims.claim: Turkesterone is a natural anabolic stronger than Dianabol
claims.believers: A forum thread cites old mouse studies that reported better results than Dianabol in mice and notes renewed popularity [21].
claims.experts: Reviews describe the supporting evidence as preclinical [3], and a small human study found no significant effect on IGF-1 or metabolic rate [4].

claims.claim: It builds muscle without suppressing your natural hormones
claims.believers: A forum poster asks for an anabolic without major suppression and suggests turkesterone and ecdysterone, comparing them to low-dose Anavar and saying they kept strength during a cut [23].
claims.experts: No study cited here measured human androgen levels or suppression with turkesterone; Wikipedia lists human effects as undetermined [1].

claims.believers: A TRT forum user says turkesterone is supposed to increase SHBG a lot and plans to add it [16].
claims.experts: No published study cited here examined SHBG.

claims.claim: Turkesterone does nothing; influencers profit from hype
claims.believers: Another forum poster states turkesterone 'doesn't do anything', adding that popular influencers who sell it claim otherwise [22].
claims.experts: A review states phytoecdysteroids lack anabolic effects in skeletal muscle in its title [5]; the human evidence is limited [4].

claims.claim: Many turkesterone products are fake or under-dosed
claims.believers: A T Nation poster warns of fakes, saying turkesterone has more of them than a related product [18].
claims.experts: No independent testing study is cited in the sources used for this article.
